Beige Book cross-check and policy read-through:

- Economic activity: District contacts reported modest-to-moderate growth, with Omicron weighing on leisure, hospitality, and some retail sales, while manufacturing and freight held up despite ongoing supply bottlenecks.
- Labor and wages: Employment continued to rise but was constrained by labor shortages and Omicron-related absenteeism. Wage pressures were broad and elevated.
- Prices: Price increases remained widespread and significant, with strong pass-through in many sectors due to persistent supply-demand imbalances.
- Credit: Banking contacts pointed to generally solid business loan demand and healthy credit quality, while residential real estate demand was mixed to softer. Standards were little changed to easier for businesses, with more caution around some consumer categories.

Policy implications relative to the FOMC statement and SLOOS:
- The Beige Book corroborates “soon appropriate” liftoff and ending net asset purchases on schedule, given persistent inflation and strong wage signals.
- However, Omicron’s near-term drag on services and softer household credit demand argue for a well-telegraphed, orderly pace of normalization and continued use of floor-system tools (IORB, ON RRP, repos) and reinvestments to maintain smooth market functioning.
- Net effect vs the SLOOS-only read: slightly tempers the hawkish tilt from strong business credit conditions, given consumer-side headwinds and virus uncertainty.

Adjusted bottom line: Still-positive/hawkish bias toward liftoff, but modestly less so than the SLOOS-only assessment.
